intro: This unit reads two suttas slowly, line by line. The first is the talk Buddhists call the first sermon, set in a deer park near Varanasi. The second is the long account of the Buddha's last journey and death. Buddhists remember one as the beginning of the teaching and the other as its passing on.

Both texts come from the Pali Canon, and both were translated by T.W. Rhys Davids in 1881. That translation is in the public domain, so you will read its exact words. You will also compare it with modern translations, and see how one Pali word can become two different English words.

By the end you will be able to explain the four noble truths as the sermon states them, trace how the Book of the Great Decease answers the question of who leads after a teacher dies, and describe how Theravada, Mahayana and modern readers read these texts. You will describe beliefs and attribute them; you will not be asked to share them.
bigQuestion: How do a tradition's accounts of its first teaching and its teacher's death shape what its followers do?

timeline.t: The Buddha is born, on many scholars' dates (Theravada tradition: 624/623 BCE)
The Buddha teaches the first sermon at Sarnath, on many scholars' dates
The Buddha's final passing at Kusinara, on many scholars' dates (tradition: 544/543 BCE)
The First Council, which tradition places soon after the Buddha's death
Ashoka sets up pillars at Sarnath and Lumbini
The Pali Canon is written down in Sri Lanka, as chronicles report
Buddhaghosa writes Pali commentaries in Sri Lanka
Rhys Davids publishes Buddhist Suttas, SBE 11
A relic vessel with an inscription is found at Piprahwa
Maurice Walshe's modern English Digha Nikaya is published

words.d: a discourse of the Buddha as the Pali Canon records it; sutra in Sanskrit
suffering, stress or unsatisfactoriness; the first noble truth
craving or thirst; the origin of suffering in the second truth
Pali for nirvana: the ending of craving and suffering
the path between pleasure-seeking and self-torment named in the first sermon
the eight parts of the path in the fourth noble truth
the three ways each truth is known in the first sermon
final nibbana; the death of an awakened person, as Buddhists describe it
formed or conditioned things, which the last words say decay
heedfulness or diligence, praised in the Buddha's last words
the code of discipline for monks and nuns

test.q: Which sutta do Buddhists call the first sermon?
test.why: The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, SN 56.11, is the first sermon.

test.q: Which sutta tells of the Buddha's last days?
test.why: Digha Nikaya 16 is the Book of the Great Decease.

test.q: What two extremes does the first sermon warn against?
test.why: The sermon opens by naming these two extremes.

test.q: What does the second noble truth name as the origin of suffering?
test.why: The second truth names tanha, craving.

test.q: Who was the first listener to understand, according to the sermon?
test.why: The eye of truth arose in Kondanna.

test.q: How many aspects does the Buddha say his knowledge of the truths had?
test.why: Four truths, each in three turnings, make twelve aspects.

test.q: Who was the Buddha's attendant who wept at Kusinara?
test.why: Ananda, the Buddha's cousin and attendant, weeps in chapter 5.

test.q: What does 'be ye lamps unto yourselves' pair with the self as a refuge?
test.why: The passage names oneself and the Dhamma as refuges.

test.q: Who served the Buddha's last meal?
test.why: Cunda at Pava served the final meal.

test.q: What quality do the Buddha's last words urge?
test.why: The last words urge appamada, diligence or heedfulness.

test.q: Why do many Mahayana traditions call the first sermon the 'first turning'?
choices: They say it was the only teaching
They describe later turnings of the wheel as well
They date it after the last days
test.why: Some Mahayana texts describe second and third turnings after the first.

test.q: Which translation of both suttas is in the public domain?
test.why: Rhys Davids' Buddhist Suttas (1881) is public domain.

test.q: Why do scholars say the suttas are full of lists and repetition?
choices: They were preserved by oral recitation
test.why: Lists and repetition supported memory in an oral tradition.

test.q: What does the sutta say should be done with the Buddha's remains?
choices: Honored in stupas, like a universal king's
test.why: The Buddha tells Ananda his remains should be treated like a universal king's, with stupas.

test.q: Which statement describes these texts in the neutral way this course uses?
choices: The gods truly proclaimed the event
The gods did not proclaim anything
The sutta says the gods proclaimed the event
Only foolish readers believe the sutta
test.why: The course describes what the text says without affirming or denying it.

write.prompt: What do these two suttas say a community should rely on when its teacher is gone? Cite two or three passages (for example SN 56.11, DN 16 2.33 and 6.1, Rhys Davids 1881), explain what each says, and describe how two Buddhist traditions read them.
tips: Name the sutta, its number and the translation for every passage you cite.
Attribute every belief: 'Theravada teachers read…', 'the sutta says…'.
Keep the Pali term beside the English the first time you use it.
Compare readings without deciding which one is right.
